name: Augustus
summary: Augustus ended the civil wars and built a monarchy in republican dress, keeping the Senate and magistracies while holding the army and decisive powers himself. He presented his rule as a restoration of ancestral custom, backing it with religious revival, marriage and morals laws, and a permanent professional army. He expanded the empire widely but left advice to keep it within existing limits.

property-fundamental.rationale: He took part in the proscriptions and land confiscations of the civil wars, but in the Res Gestae he claims he was the first to pay for lands assigned to veterans, buying estates in Italy and the provinces.

strong-leader.rationale: Suetonius reports he twice considered restoring the republic but concluded it would be dangerous to leave the state in the hands of more than one man, so he kept it; the Res Gestae presents his settlement as ending civil war.

state-harmful.rationale: The Res Gestae lists the aqueducts, roads, temples, grain and cash distributions and the military treasury he built or paid for, so his record is of building up the state he headed, not of abolishing government.

reviewHistory.rationale: He built up state institutions on a large scale (army, guard, fire and police services, treasury, road network) and ruled as their head.

traditional-family.rationale: Suetonius reports that he revised and enacted laws on adultery and chastity and on the encouragement of marriage among the classes, and pressed the marriage law against open resistance until he softened part of it.

reviewHistory.rationale: He personally drove the marriage and morality legislation (the Julian marriage law and the later Papia Poppaea law, with penalties for the unmarried and childless and rewards for parents, and the law against adultery) to strengthen marriage and family life.

more-religion-public.rationale: He rebuilt 82 temples in Rome, built or restored many more, revived neglected rites (Lupercalia, Secular Games, Compitalia, augury of Safety), and increased the number, privileges and income of priests.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: In the Res Gestae he states that by new laws he restored many ancestral traditions that were falling out of use; he also revived old rites and festivals and ordered the toga worn in the Forum.

gradual-change.rationale: He states in the Res Gestae that he refused any office offered to him that was contrary to ancestral custom, and he kept republican forms and magistracies while concentrating power in himself.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: He avoided the titles of king, dictator and lord and framed his rule as a restored republic, while building a de facto hereditary principate; the evidence points both ways.

separate-church-state.rationale: He held the chief priesthood (pontifex maximus) himself together with other priestly offices while ruling, and ran state religion as part of the state, with public games, vows and sacrifices decreed by the Senate.

military-superiority.rationale: He boasts of conquests, of forcing the Parthians to return Roman standards and seek friendship, and of embassies from distant kings; Roman power over all rivals was his stated achievement.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Suetonius reports that his marriage laws obliged citizens to marry and rear children under penalties, and that he pressed them against resistance, placing the community's aim ahead of individual choice.

reviewHistory.rationale: His marriage and morals laws imposed duties on citizens to marry and have children, with penalties for evasion, placing the community's needs ahead of individual choice.

harm-principle.rationale: Suetonius reports that he enacted laws on extravagance, adultery and chastity, and regulated dress and seating, restricting adult conduct that harmed no one else.

reviewHistory.rationale: He legislated private morals and conduct for adults through laws on extravagance, adultery and chastity, and marriage, and regulated dress and seating, which goes beyond preventing harm to others.

conscription.rationale: Dio reports that after the Varian disaster, when no men of military age enrolled, he made them draw lots, stripped every fifth man under thirty-five and every tenth older man of property and civil rights, and put some who still refused to death; Suetonius adds that he sold a knight who maimed his sons to avoid service.

territorial-expansion.rationale: In the Res Gestae (ch. 26-27) he lists extending the boundaries of the provinces bordering unsubdued peoples, the addition of Egypt, Pannonia and others, and campaigns reaching the Elbe, the Danube and Arabia.

reviewHistory.rationale: The Res Gestae records that he extended the frontiers of all provinces bordering unconquered peoples and added Egypt, Pannonia and others; Tacitus reports that his last written advice recommended keeping the empire within its present limits, so late evidence points the other way.

reviewHistory.rationale: He set up statues of Rome's great men so that rulers would measure up to them and says he set precedents for posterity, but he also legislated heavily on morals with penalties; the evidence points both ways.

national-self-determination.rationale: He conquered and annexed many peoples, though in some cases (Armenia, per the Res Gestae) he preferred to hand the kingdom to a client king instead of making it a province; the king was one he chose.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Suetonius reports he took omens and dreams seriously and feared thunder, carrying a sealskin as protection; he did not rely on reason alone.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: The Res Gestae records that he restored eighty-two temples, the Capitol, Pompey's theatre and the aqueducts and completed his father's buildings; Suetonius says he left Rome in marble.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: He legislated seating that kept women to the upper rows at shows and had his daughter and granddaughters taught spinning and weaving, and his marriage laws treated women's status in terms of marriage and children; none of this is a statement about public roles.

night-watchman-state.rationale: He greatly extended the state: grain distributions, public building, aqueducts, roads, fire brigades, a state military treasury and legislation on marriage, dress and morals.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: He legislated rank and status distinctions: citizenship granted sparingly, limits on manumission, separate seating by order, and marriage restrictions between orders, so equality before the law was not his policy.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: The Res Gestae (ch. 26-30) lists the wars he began or directed against peoples on the frontiers (Alpine tribes, Pannonians, Dacians, Germans, Arabia) as achievements.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Suetonius reports that as triumvir he pressed the 43 BC proscriptions, which outlawed hundreds of senators and knights without trial, and was more insistent than his colleagues that no one be spared.

reviewHistory.rationale: The armies swore their oath to him, he commanded the legions through his own deputies (legati) and set up the Praetorian Guard, and he appointed the prefects and provincial governors who ran the imperial provinces.

people-in-arms.rationale: In the Res Gestae (ch. 17) he lists his payments into the military treasury for rewards to soldiers on completing their service, which funded a professional standing army in place of citizen levies.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Rather than curbing religious institutions he increased the number and importance of priests and their allowances and privileges, especially the Vestals, though he also took the chief priesthood into his own hands and culled prophetic books.

sacred-ruler.rationale: He took the title son of the deified and the name Augustus, and Suetonius reports that his person was made sacred by law, but he refused to be called lord and accepted worship only jointly with Rome.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: In the Res Gestae he claims he held no more power than his colleagues in any magistracy and refused powers contrary to ancestral custom; Suetonius adds that he wanted even his friends bound by the same laws, though his actual power was far wider than this claim.

leader-cult.rationale: He accepted honours such as the title Father of the Country, a golden shield and the name Augustus, yet he removed about eighty silver statues of himself from Rome, refused to be called lord and checked public flattery, so the evidence points both ways.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: By order of the people and Senate he increased the number of patricians, and he kept rank-based privileges such as reserved seating for senators and knights; he kept hereditary orders in being rather than abolishing them.

elective-rulers.rationale: He arranged his own succession by adoption and family designation (Gaius and Lucius, then Tiberius) instead of leaving the choice of ruler to election, although Senate and people formally acclaimed his offices.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The Res Gestae (ch. 34) records that in 27 BC he handed the republic to the Senate and people, yet he went on holding tribunician power every year and imperium in the provinces, and drove major legislation himself, so his record points both ways.

arms-reduction.rationale: After the civil wars he discharged and settled several hundred thousand soldiers (Res Gestae 3) but kept a permanent army; whether that was only the minimum needed for safety is not settled by the record.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: Suetonius reports that his laws rewarded married parents, penalised celibacy, and revived and funded old rites and priesthoods, so the state backed the ways of life he judged good.

notes: Later pass (rules 7) on the 2026-10-23 audit. Answers rest on the Res Gestae (his own record of his acts, tagged as actions), Suetonius, Tacitus and Cassius Dio, read in full from the local copies; answers that cited Wikipedia were rewritten from Suetonius or the Res Gestae, and one (individual pension accounts) was nulled because the military treasury does not settle it. Added: conscription (Dio, Suetonius), starting wars, abolishing legal marriage, state support for good ways of life. Themes searched in the texts and left null where nothing settles them: economy and taxation (the 5 percent inheritance tax and grain dole do not settle heavy inheritance tax or welfare cuts), money and banking, courts and juries, federalism, immigration and citizenship (Suetonius on stinginess with citizenship does not settle citizenship by descent), religion and conversion, speech and censorship (his libel measures do not settle hate-speech law), international arbitration and alliances. Cassius Dio book 52 (the Agrippa and Maecenas debate) is Dio's own composition and was not used. His own written advice to keep the empire within its limits (Tacitus, Annals 1.11) is words and does not outweigh the record of conquest.
